name: ml-competition-ai-rules-census
made_by: MV2 of Munim, Inc., with AI agents working in his name
method: For each platform or contest the platform-wide terms page (or, where none exists, the standard per-competition rules template or the platform's own documentation) was fetched on 2026-10-17 and searched for: AI-assisted or AI-generated code; AutoML; commercial LLM APIs inside a solution; external data; pre-trained models; whether companies or legal entities may enter; age and sanctions; winner code terms; reproducibility audits. Quotes are verbatim fragments of at most 125 characters each. 'read_how' says whether the primary page was read directly, read from a saved copy, extracted from a PDF by code, or only seen through search-result snippets. On 2026-10-18 EvalAI's public JSON list of running challenges (https://eval.ai/api/challenges/challenge/present/approved/public, 18 challenges; the upcoming list https://eval.ai/api/challenges/challenge/future/approved/public was empty) was searched in every field for placeholder text ('Lorem', 'ipsum', 'consectetur', 'dolor sit'), in the terms fields for AI-tool terms, and its has_prize flags were counted; the challenges that stood out were re-read from https://eval.ai/api/challenges/challenge/<id>. On 2026-10-21 Zindi's public competition list (https://api.zindi.world/v1/competitions, first page of 20, 7 open of 515 listed) was taken, and the JSON of all 7 open competitions plus 2 recently closed ones was fetched from https://api.zindi.world/v1/competitions/<slug> and searched for LLM coding tools, development assistants, AI tools, generative AI, ChatGPT, AutoML, paid APIs, proprietary model services and disclosure of AI use; the platform rules page https://zindi.world/rules was re-fetched the same day. Also on 2026-10-21 the ARC Prize 2026 overview page was fetched and added as a contest record, and the official rules PDF of the U.S. DOE GEMS Prize (linked from its DrivenData rules tab through HeroX resource 2274) was downloaded in a sealed job, its text extracted per page with PyMuPDF 1.28.2 and searched by code for the same topics (artificial intelligence, AI, generative, LLM, ChatGPT, AutoML, eligibility, entity, individual, citizen, licence, intellectual property, open source, deadline, prize amounts); the pages with hits were then read in full. On 2026-10-21 three more DOE prize rules PDFs were chosen from their HeroX prize and resource pages and fixed in order, with two predictions written down before any of their text was read (see doe_template_check_2026_10_22); they were downloaded and searched by the same code in a sealed job and graded on 2026-10-22. Long JSON pages were read by a text-extraction model in parts of 100,000 characters.
headline: No platform-wide terms of 13 platforms or contests read have a clause on AI-assisted or AI-generated code. Clauses exist only at competition level, and three have now been found. Two PERMIT AI help in writing the entry. The U.S. DOE GEMS Prize ($300,000, on DrivenData, rules dated September 2026) allows generative AI for every submission element and is the only ML competition found that REQUIRES entrants to disclose the extent and manner of their AI use. The same duty, in nearly the same words, is in 2 of 3 other DOE prize rules read for comparison (Energy Storage Innovations Prize Round 2, amended 2025-12-12 to add it, and Digitizing Utilities Prize Round 3, rewritten 2026-01-08); there the disclosure goes in a 'technical concept paper' or 'narrative' that the entry must contain, so the GEMS clause is shared DOE prize text and its undefined 'narrative' most likely came with it. One Zindi competition, the Bias Bounty Mapping Equity Challenge (rules updated 2026-10-06), says commercial LLM coding tools may be used for drafting, debugging, testing and documentation, provided the submitted solution does not need them to run or reproduce, and asks for no disclosure; it is 1 of the 7 open Zindi competitions on 2026-10-21, and the other 6 use Zindi's standard text, which says only open-source languages and tools may be used 'in building models' and does not separate a coding assistant from a modelling tool. The third clause (eBay 2026 University ML Competition - Canada, on EvalAI) restricts data and output licensing, not authorship. The rules that otherwise bind an AI-made entry stay indirect: natural-person-only eligibility (Kaggle; DrivenData's standard template, which GEMS overrides for U.S. companies), open-source / no-paid-service / no-internet rules that keep commercial LLM APIs out of the solution itself (Zindi, bitgrit, ARC Prize 2026 on Kaggle), and reproducibility audits (NeurIPS EEG/EMG 2026, bitgrit, Zindi, GEMS).

changes.what: Checked whether the GEMS generative-AI clause is shared DOE prize text. Three other DOE prize rules PDFs were fixed in advance (Energy Storage Innovations Prize Round 2, Digitizing Utilities Prize Round 3, Industrial Energy Storage Systems Prize) with two predictions written before any text was read: P1, at least one has a generative-AI clause (guess 50%); P2, if so it requires disclosure rather than banning AI (guess 65%). Both held: 2 of 3 carry the clause, both as 'not prohibited' plus a 'must indicate' disclosure duty. In both, the disclosure goes into a defined part of the entry (a technical concept paper; a 2,500-word narrative), so the 'narrative' left undefined in the GEMS rules most likely came over from this shared text. The Energy Storage rules list 'Incorporate guidance about the use of generative artificial intelligence' among the changes of their 2025-12-12 amendment. The third document, which has no change table, has no AI clause. These three are hardware and utility prizes, not ML competitions, so they sit under doe_template_check_2026_10_22 and are not counted as platform records.

Added the U.S. DOE GEMS Prize (Geologic Enhanced Mapping System, $300,000, hosted on DrivenData) from its 19-page official rules PDF, text extracted by code. It permits generative AI in developing every submission element and requires entrants to disclose 'the extent to which, if any' they used it and how: the first disclosure duty in the census. The disclosure is to go 'in the narrative', a submission element defined nowhere else in the rules and not asked for on the competition's DrivenData pages. GEMS admits U.S.-incorporated private entities, so DrivenData's natural-persons-only rule is a template default, not a platform rule. The site deadline (Dec. 3, 2026, 11:59 p.m. UTC) and the rules' '5:00 p.m. ET on the prize submission deadline date' differ by about two hours. Wording corrected: 0.3.0 called the Zindi Bias Bounty clause the first explicit permission; GEMS's rules are dated September 2026, before the Bias Bounty update of 2026-10-06, so it was only the first one this census found.

Zindi competition-level check: all 7 open competitions plus 2 recently closed ones. One (bias-bounty-mapping-equity-challenge) has the first explicit clause found that permits AI-assisted code: commercial LLM coding tools allowed for drafting, debugging, testing and documentation if the solution does not depend on them. The other 8 carry Zindi's standard text ('You may only use open-source languages and tools in building models for this challenge.') and no AI-tool clause. Zindi's platform rules page re-fetched: still no AI-tool clause. Added ARC Prize 2026 (no internet in Kaggle evaluation, so no GPT/Claude API inside a solution; prize code must be open source under CC0 or MIT-0). Headline rewritten: '0 clauses' now holds for platform-wide terms only.

Checked all 18 running public EvalAI challenges: none ships the starter template's Lorem ipsum terms; none has has_prize true, though one (id 2672) lists $1,500 in cash prizes in its description while its terms say 'There are no prizes.' and its API end_date (2099) disagrees with its stated deadline (May 31, 2026); one (id 2680, eBay, Canadian students) has an explicit 'Use of AI' section about data and licensing.

Added EvalAI (host documentation and starter template) and CrunchDAO (documentation landing page). Re-tried Numerai, Signate, Topcoder and HeroX: their terms pages were JS-only, redirected or missing, so they stay under not_covered with the reason.
First census: Zindi, AIcrowd, DrivenData, Kaggle, Codabench, NeurIPS 2026 EEG/EMG Foundation Challenge, Wunder Fund Alfa Connectome, ThinkOnward, bitgrit.

ai_clause.where: Section 3.2 'Process Overview', bullet 'Indication of use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) technology, if applicable' (page 9)
quotes: Using generative AI technology in the development of your prize submission is allowed.
you must indicate in the narrative (not included in the word count)
the extent to which, if any, you used generative AI technology and how you used it to develop your submission
including all submission elements described in this official rules document
You are responsible for the accuracy, authenticity, and authorship representations of your submission
Relying on generative AI may introduce significant risks
ai_clause.reading: permits generative AI for every submission element, which includes the code assets finalists hand over, and is the only rule in this census that REQUIRES AI use to be disclosed (its extent and how). The word 'narrative' occurs once in the 19 pages; section 3.5 'What To Submit' lists predictions, code assets and documentation, and the DrivenData competition pages ask for no narrative or write-up, so where the disclosure should go is not defined. The wording follows the U.S. National Science Foundation's notice of 2023-12-14 to grant proposers, which encourages rather than requires disclosure. 0.3.2 found the same clause in two other DOE prize rules, where 'the narrative' is a defined part of the entry (see doe_template_check_2026_10_22).

platforms.note: Prize: $300,000; Phase 1 $50,000 'Split equally among top five winners', Phase 2 $250,000 ($100,000 / $70,000 / $40,000 / $25,000 / $15,000). Deadline mismatch: the competition page gives 'Dec. 3, 2026, 11:59 p.m. UTC'; rules section A.1 requires entries 'by 5:00 p.m. ET on the prize submission deadline date' (11:59 p.m. UTC is 6:59 p.m. EST). Registrants certify eligibility 'under penalty of perjury'. Prize goals (page 7) ask that a submission confirm the competitor's 'intent to commercialize early-stage technology and establish a viable U.S.-based business in the near future', apparently shared American-Made text.

doe_template_check_2026_10_22.question: Is the GEMS generative-AI clause shared U.S. DOE prize text? Three DOE prize rules documents (hardware and utility prizes on HeroX, not ML competitions) were read for comparison only.
doe_template_check_2026_10_22.preregistered: Written 2026-10-21 before any of the three texts was read; documents fixed in order D1, D2, D3 the same day; a document that failed to download would have been skipped, not counted. P1: at least one of the documents has a clause on generative AI or AI tools (guess 50%). P2: if so, it requires disclosure rather than banning AI use (guess 65%). Only rules text extracted by code counts; HeroX page text does not.
doe_template_check_2026_10_22.result: P1 held: 2 of 3 have the clause (D1, D2). P2 held: both permit generative AI ('not prohibited') and require entrants to state the extent and manner of its use; neither bans it.
doe_template_check_2026_10_22.how_read: Each PDF downloaded in a sealed job filed on 2026-10-21, with the same extraction code as GEMS (PyMuPDF 1.28.2, per-page text, keyword counts by code); pages with AI hits and each document's preface read in full on 2026-10-22.

doe_template_check_2026_10_22.reading: The GEMS clause is shared DOE prize text, not a one-off: three of the four DOE prize rules now read carry it, in nearly the same words ('the extent to which, if any', 'not included in the word count', 'accuracy, authenticity, and authorship representations', 'Reliance on generative AI may introduce significant risks'). D1 and D2 write in the third person ('not prohibited'); GEMS writes in the second person ('allowed'). In D1 and D2 the disclosure goes into a written document the entry must contain (a technical concept paper; a 2,500-word narrative). D2's wording 'must indicate in the narrative (not included in the word count)' is the one GEMS uses, but GEMS, a leaderboard competition on DrivenData, asks for no narrative, so the GEMS gap most likely came from reusing this text unchanged. That is an inference from wording; DOE's drafting history was not seen. D1 dates the clause's arrival: its 2025-12-12 amendment lists 'Incorporate guidance about the use of generative artificial intelligence' among its substantive changes. D3, the only document without a change table, is the only one without the clause, consistent with (not proof of) the clause entering DOE prize rules through amendments from December 2025 on. Four documents are a small sample.

limits: Platform terms were read on one date (2026-10-17), EvalAI's live list one day later, Zindi's competitions, ARC Prize 2026 and the DOE GEMS Prize on 2026-10-21, and three more DOE prize rules on 2026-10-22. Rules change; per-competition rules can override every platform-wide term quoted here.
Kaggle quotes come from search-result snippets of rules pages, not from a direct read; Kaggle's pages are JS-rendered.

The EvalAI and CrunchDAO records rest on documentation pages, not on binding terms: EvalAI has no platform-wide participation terms, and CrunchDAO's per-competition rules were not read. The ARC Prize record rests on the overview page, not on each track's detailed rules.

The EvalAI live check covers only challenges in the public 'present/approved' list on 2026-10-18; private, unapproved and past challenges were not checked. The long JSON list was read in two parts by a text-search model, and the three challenges discussed (2266, 2672, 2680) were re-read one by one.

The Zindi check covers the 7 open competitions and 2 closed ones, not Zindi's 515 listed competitions. Three of the long competition JSON pages were read only to 100,000 characters; the unread rest held repeated copies of parent-competition rules. The JSON was read by a text-extraction model, not parsed by code.

GEMS is the only ML competition with DOE rules in this census. Four DOE prize rules have now been read (GEMS plus three for comparison), out of many more DOE prizes; the three were chosen because their rules PDFs could be found, not at random. Pages without keyword hits (table of contents and background) were not all read in full. That the GEMS 'narrative' came over from shared text is an inference from wording.
Quotes are fragments of at most 125 characters, so some sentences are split; the URL gives the full text.

Absence of a clause is reported as 'not addressed', never as 'allowed'. Whether Zindi reads its standard 'open-source languages and tools in building models' sentence as covering coding assistants is not known; only the organisers can say.
